q: The payment of compensation to railway employees by the railway administration for injury by accident is governed by:

options.C: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016

e: The correct answer is The Employees Compensation Act, 1923. Compensation for injury by accident to railway employees is governed by the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 (originally the Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923, renamed in 2009). The Act makes the railway administration liable to pay compensation for personal injury caused by an accident arising out of and in the course of employment. Railway servants are expressly covered in the Act's Schedule II, which lists the employees to whom the Act applies.

q: In case of death of a railway servant due to accidents arising out of and in the course of employment, compensation will be paid to the dependents as defined in
e: Option C (The Employees Compensation Act 1923) is the correct choice. On the death of a railway servant in an accident arising out of and in the course of employment, compensation goes to the 'dependants' as defined in Section 2 of the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923. The Act's definition covers the widow, minor children, and other relatives such as a widowed mother who were wholly or partly dependent on the deceased's earnings. Only persons falling within this statutory definition can claim. Payment to anyone outside the defined list is not valid compensation under the Act.

q: Employment of children is prohibited in occupations and processes mentioned in

options.A: Schedule of Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act
options.B: Schedule of Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act
options.C: Schedule-II of Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act

e: Schedule of Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act — that is the right answer. Employment of children is prohibited in the occupations and processes set out in the Schedule to the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 — this is stated in Section 3 of the Act. The Schedule lists hazardous occupations and processes where no child below 14 may be employed. Railway workshops and factories must respect this prohibition alongside the Factories Act's age bar.

q: The appropriate Government shall review or revise minimum rate of wages ordinarily at an interval not exceeding years.
e: Option B () 5 years) is the correct choice. The appropriate government must review or revise minimum rates of wages at intervals not exceeding five years under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. This five-year ceiling ensures wages keep pace with the cost of living. The Act covers scheduled employments, and railway employment is among the scheduled employments where the Central Government is the appropriate government. Note: the Act recognises only four worker categories — unskilled, semi-skilled, skilled and highly skilled.

q: In terms of Minimum Wages Act, which of the following is NOT a category of workers?
e: The correct answer is Expert. Under the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the recognised categories of workers are unskilled, semi-skilled, skilled and highly skilled — 'Expert' is NOT a statutory category. Minimum wage rates are fixed separately for each of these four categories in scheduled employments. This is a favourite exam trap because 'expert' sounds plausible. Remember also that wages must be reviewed at intervals not exceeding five years under the same Act.

q: The Factories Act 1948 impose statutory obligation on the Railway Administrations to provide and maintain canteens in Railway Establishments, which are governed by the Factories Act and employ more than 250 persons. The provision of canteen in all other Railway Establishments is provided under:
e: None of the above — that is the right answer. A statutory canteen obligation arises only under Section 46 of the Factories Act, 1948, which applies to factory-governed railway establishments employing more than 250 persons. Canteens in all other railway establishments are provided administratively as a staff welfare measure — not under the Organised Workers Social Security Act, the Railway Act, 1989, or the Employees' Compensation Act — so 'None of the above' is correct. Exam tip: Section 46's 250-worker threshold is one of the most-asked figures from this Act.

q: To which settlement machinery can the central government refer the disputes under rule 81-A?
e: The correct answer is Adjudicator. Under Rule 81-A, industrial disputes were referred for adjudication — that is, to an adjudicator such as an industrial tribunal or labour court — rather than to conciliation or arbitration machinery. Rule 81-A of the wartime Defence of India Rules created this compulsory reference system for preventing and settling disputes. It became the foundation of the adjudication machinery later carried into the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Remember the trio under the ID Act: conciliation, arbitration and adjudication.

q: Schedule II of the Employees Compensation Act 1923 deals with

options.A: Age factor for calculating the amount of compensation
options.B: List of persons who are included in the definition of ‘Employee’
options.D: List of injuries Deemed to Result in Permanent Total Disablement

e: List of persons who are included in the definition of ‘Employee’ — that is the right answer. Schedule II of the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 contains the list of persons included in the definition of 'employee' — railway servants are expressly among them. This Schedule fixes who the Act covers. The other Schedules do different jobs: Schedule I lists injuries deemed to result in permanent total disablement, and Schedule III lists occupational diseases. Exam tip: questions often jumble these Schedules, so map them — I for disablement injuries, II for employees, III for diseases.

q: How many members does a conciliation board consists of as per the appropriate government?
e: Chairman and 2 or 4 other members — that is the right answer. A Board of Conciliation under Section 5 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 consists of a chairman and two or four other members, as the appropriate government thinks fit. The members represent the workmen and the employer in equal numbers. The board's job is to bring about a settlement of the dispute referred to it. Related exam fact: a Court of Inquiry under Section 6 is headed by an independent person — the composition pattern of 'chairman plus equal representation' is the board's signature feature.

q: GST is a consumption of goods and service tax based on
e: Option D (Destination) is the correct choice. GST is a destination-based consumption tax — it is levied where goods and services are consumed, not where they are produced. This is the core design difference from the old origin-based taxes like excise duty. For railways this matters: freight tax accrues to the destination state. Related exam fact: IGST (Integrated GST) is the mechanism that handles inter-state supplies and transfers the revenue to the consuming state.

q: The number of structures in India’s GST model is?
e: 4 — that is the right answer. India's GST model has four structures — CGST, SGST, IGST and UTGST. CGST and SGST apply on intra-state supplies (Centre and State respectively), IGST on inter-state supplies, and UTGST on supplies within Union Territories without legislatures. This four-fold structure flows from the dual model borrowed from Canada. Related exam fact: the maximum rate fixed for CGST is 20% under the CGST Act.

q: The maximum rate for CGST is?
e: 20 — that is the right answer. The maximum rate for CGST is 20% — the CGST Act fixes 20% as the ceiling, with the actual rates notified by the GST Council (the standard slabs being 0%, 5%, 12%, 18% and 28% at launch). CGST is the Centre's share on intra-state supplies. Related exam fact: SGST/UTGST carry the same 20% ceiling, while IGST — which combines both — has a 40% ceiling. The principle behind this is worth grasping, not just memorising: once you understand why the rule is framed this way, the answer follows naturally instead of needing rote recall.

q: Which of the following tax was abolished by GST?
e: Service tax — that is the right answer. GST abolished service tax — it was one of the major Central indirect taxes subsumed into GST from 1st July 2017, along with excise duty, CVD, SAD and State VAT. This is why railway passenger and freight services moved from service tax to GST. Corporation tax, income tax and wealth tax are direct taxes and were untouched by GST. Related exam fact: the 101st Constitutional Amendment, 2016 enabled this overhaul.

q: Which constitutional amendment has been done to pass the GST bill?
e: The GST was enacted through the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 — the 122nd was the number of the Constitutional Amendment Bill, 2014, not of the enacted amendment. It inserted Articles 246A, 269A and 279A and created the GST Council; GST was rolled out on 1 July 2017.

q: Goods and service tax is ____.
e: The correct answer is Consumption based. GST is consumption-based — it is a destination-based tax on the consumption of goods and services, levied where they are consumed rather than where they are supplied or produced. This is the single most-tested conceptual point about GST. Related exam fact: IGST is the instrument that carries tax revenue to the consuming state on inter-state supplies, keeping the destination principle intact.
